planting.note: Pot in a chunky, well-aerated aroid mix and provide a moss pole or bark totem; this species produces its most dramatic lobed foliage once established as a climber.

directions: Native to the wet forests of Colombia and Ecuador, this climbing aroid produces narrow, deeply dissected leaf blades cut almost to the midrib into slender, feather-like segments, a texture unlike any other Monstera grown as a houseplant. Train young plants onto a moss pole or bark slab, since contact with a climbing surface pushes the vine toward larger, more deeply cut adult leaves instead of the smaller, less lobed juvenile form. Keep the chunky, free-draining mix evenly moist through the growing season but let the top layer dry slightly between waterings, and provide bright, indirect light with high humidity for the fastest growth. Protect from temperatures below 55F and keep out of direct sun, which scorches the thin leaf segments.

planting.note: Grow in a chunky aroid mix with a moss pole or coir support; mature leaves become far more deeply cut when the vine is allowed to climb rather than trail.

directions: A hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid of Central American rainforests, Monstera dissecta develops elongated, oval leaf blades that split progressively from the margin toward the midrib as the plant matures, creating an airy, lace-like silhouette distinct from the rounder fenestrations of M. adansonii. Juvenile leaves are nearly solid, so patience and a climbing support are both needed to coax the plant into its signature dissected adult form. Water when the top half of the chunky, well-draining substrate has dried, and provide bright indirect light, warmth above 60F, and humidity of 50% or higher for best growth. It is an uncommon species in cultivation, so source nursery-propagated plants from reputable aroid specialists.
sources: Houseplant Authority — Monstera Dissecta Care Guide

planting.note: Grow in a semi-coarse, fast-draining aroid mix with a sturdy climbing support to encourage full-sized, heavily fenestrated adult leaves.

directions: Named for the municipality of Acacoyagua in Chiapas, Mexico, where it was first collected, this climbing Monstera produces large, broadly fenestrated, glossy green leaves that develop substantial holes and splits as the vine matures and gains size. It tolerates somewhat lower light than many other large-leaved Monstera species, making it more forgiving in average indoor settings, though a bright spot still produces the biggest, most deeply perforated foliage. Water once the top two inches of soil have dried, and provide a climbing support so the vine can reach the size needed to produce its characteristic fenestrations. Keep above 55F and avoid soggy, waterlogged mix.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-draining aroid mix with a moss pole for support.

directions: One of the more recently described Monstera species, found only in Costa Rica, M. juliusii is distinguished by mottled, whitish-green leaf stems and a persistent, papery cataphyll sheath that clasps the stem below each new leaf, giving the growing tip a distinctive feather-like texture. Mature leaves are elongated and glossy green, carried on a slender climbing stem that is more modest in scale than M. deliciosa. Allow the top portion of the chunky substrate to dry between waterings, keep humidity at 50% or higher, and provide a moss pole or stake, since the plant's size and leaf display improve markedly once it has something to climb. Protect from direct sun and from temperatures below 55F.
sources: The Nature of Home — Monstera Juliusii Plant Care Guide
Research on Monstera (Araceae) of Costa Rica, Croat et al.

planting.note: Grow in a cool-leaning, humid indoor spot with a moss pole; this cloud-forest species prefers slightly cooler nights than lowland Monstera species.

directions: Native to the cloud forests of Costa Rica's Cordillera de Tilaran and Guanacaste mountains near Monteverde, this climbing aroid produces large, deeply pinnatifid leaves with up to eight lobes per side and occasional fenestrations away from the midrib, reaching up to two feet long on mature plants. Because it comes from cooler, misty, high-elevation cloud forest rather than hot lowland jungle, it appreciates slightly cooler temperatures and consistently high humidity compared to many other Monstera species, and resents hot, dry indoor air. Grow in bright indirect light with a moss pole or bark support, water when the top of the chunky mix has dried, and avoid temperatures below 55F. It remains an uncommon species outside specialist aroid collections, so source cutting-grown plants from reputable tropical plant nurseries.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online — Monstera monteverdensis M.Cedeno & Croat
